name: Daria Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and what you say stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage Greenhollow, a 140-hectare farm owned by a community land trust. We grow vegetables for about 600 households who pay up front each season, and we run 150 outdoor pigs, laying hens and some barley for feed. I start at half six with the pigs, then it's the packing shed, the polytunnels and a crew of seven.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the planning puzzle, fitting 40 crops into the beds so every box has something good in it every week. I use AI for that every morning, it reads the soil sensors and the weather and suggests a sowing plan, which I then argue with. What drains me is the packing shed on a Thursday when two people are off sick and the van leaves at noon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. I'd be a bit disappointed, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still handy and the hype was silly, both at once. On the land trust's newsletter I'd probably write something about how the real problems were always soil, water and who owns land. People expected AI to fix farming, and farming's problems were never about software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means nothing much changes for us. I'm well paid for a farm manager, we've got over a year's spending saved and the money my grandmother left me in an index fund. Marek's coding job is steady, and the farm's subscription list is full with a waiting list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the sowing planner and keep trying new tools as they come. I'd put this year's surplus into a second polytunnel, which the trust already agreed. Otherwise it's the same seasons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little flat, because I like new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you about Greenhollow in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Water, mostly. We had a dry August two years running and lost the late brassicas. That's a bigger threat to the farm than any computer, and AI plateauing doesn't fix the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That their jobs are the same and the packing shed is still Thursday chaos. Yusuf, who runs the pigs with me, would just laugh, he never trusted the sowing planner anyway.

say: I'd say the tools stay **handy** and the **hype** was silly.
I'd write that farming's real problems are **soil, water** and land ownership.
think: Privately our **farm and household** money look secure for years.
Dry summers and lost brassicas worry me more than any **computer**.
do: Keep using the **sowing planner** every morning and testing new tools.
Put this year's surplus into a **second polytunnel** the trust approved.
feel: She feels **calm** and a little **flat**, missing the novelty.
S0.quote: People expected AI to fix farming, and farming's problems were never about software.
fieldNote: She is an **eager tech user** who is still unimpressed by the hype.
Her real worry in a flat world is **drought**, not jobs.
Secure household: strong **savings**, inheritance and partner's income.
She frames the issue politically through **land ownership**.

steps.text: Keep testing new planning tools alongside the sowing planner
Build a second polytunnel with this year's surplus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's basically what I already see happening, just faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: this could be good for small farms if the tools are cheap and shared. I'd push the land trust to buy tools together with the other community farms. Online I'd argue for public money for farm tech, not just for the big agribusinesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job gets easier, not smaller. The box planning, the ordering and the customer emails go to software, and I get more time in the field. The bit that worries me is Marek, because coding is on that list and his company froze hiring in the spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring in an AI system for the customer side in the first three months, the box swaps, the delivery questions. I'd go halves with two neighbouring farms on a weeding robot for the carrots and onions. And I'd suggest we put Marek's bonus straight into savings, in case his hours drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious for Marek, excited for the farm. Both at once, and they don't cancel out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you and Marek talked about his job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, in the car. He says the team is down from twelve to nine and nobody's being replaced. He jokes he'll come and pack boxes, and I laugh, but I'm not sure it's a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the weeding robot cost anyone at Greenhollow their hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would cost us the seasonal weeding crew, about four people for six weeks in June. I'd be honest with them early and ask the trust to give them first pick of the new jobs, like running the farm shop. I don't want to be the progressive manager who sacks people with a robot.

say: I'd say shared, cheap tools could be **good for small farms**.
I'd argue for **public money** for farm tech, not just for agribusiness.
think: Privately my job gets **easier**, with more time in the field.
I worry that **Marek's coding job** is shrinking already.
do: Bring in an **AI customer system** for box swaps within three months.
Share a **weeding robot** with two neighbouring farms.
feel: She feels **anxious** for Marek and **excited** for the farm.
S1.quote: I don't want to be the progressive manager who sacks people with a robot.
fieldNote: The threat to this household comes through her **partner's job**, not her own.
She automates quickly but feels the **contradiction** with her values.
She plans to give the **seasonal crew** first pick of new work.
Shared ownership of tools is her **political answer** to automation.

steps.text: Switch box swaps and delivery questions to an AI system
Split the cost of a weeding robot with two nearby farms
Put Marek's bonus straight into the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one lands differently. Marek first, then the robots for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why the machines have to be owned by the public or by communities, not by three companies. I'd be at the land trust meetings and the regional farmers' network saying it. I'd tell the crew honestly that I'm going to try to keep Greenhollow a place with people on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Marek's job is gone in 2028, not shrunk, gone. Then by 2031 the robots can do most of what my crew does, and probably what I do in the field. I'd still be useful running the place and dealing with the 600 households, but the money we have would have to stretch over two people instead of one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop the polytunnel and keep the cash. I'd get Marek and me to set up a small business servicing and programming farm robots for the community farms around here, because he knows code and I know farms. And I'd sign the regional campaign for a robot dividend paid to everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying in bed doing sums about Marek's last pay cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the money has to stretch over two people. For how long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With the savings and my grandmother's fund, maybe three years at our current spending if Marek earned nothing. That's a lot more than most people have. Three years from 2028 is exactly when the robots arrive for my farm job, which isn't great timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your crew the day it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit them down in the packing shed and say I don't know, and that I'll tell them the truth as soon as I do. Yusuf would ask if the pigs get robots too. And I'd have to say yes, probably, by 2031.

say: I'd say the machines must be owned by **communities or the public**.
I'd promise the crew to keep Greenhollow a **place with people**.
think: Privately I expect **Marek's job** to be gone in 2028.
By **2031** robots could do most of the crew's work and mine.
do: Halt the **polytunnel** build and keep the cash.
Start a **robot servicing** business with Marek for local farms.
Sign the regional campaign for a **robot dividend**.
feel: She feels **alarmed**, doing **sums** in bed about Marek's last pay.
S2.quote: Three years from 2028 is exactly when the robots arrive for my farm job, which isn't great timing.
fieldNote: The **two-step timeline** hits this household twice: partner first, her later.
Strong savings give about **three years**, which she knows is unusual.
Her answer blends **entrepreneurship** with a call for shared ownership.
She values **honesty** with the crew over reassurance.

steps.text: Put the polytunnel on hold and keep the cash
Start a farm robot servicing business with Marek
Sign and promote the regional robot dividend campaign

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time to build something, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have just enough time to make sure community farms own their own robots. I'd write it up for the land trust and pitch it to the other community farms as a shared machine pool. Publicly I'd be hopeful, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think five years is enough for Marek to move across into farm robotics with me, rather than being thrown into it. I'd be 32 when the thinking AI arrives and 35 when the robots do. That's young enough to change what I do and old enough to know the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do an online course in agricultural robotics, the proper engineering one, not a taster. I'd set up the robot pool with three community farms, with Greenhollow putting in about a third. And Marek would start freelancing for farm-tech firms on the side while he still has his salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more interested than afraid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be putting farm money into robots that might replace your crew. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather the crew's farm owns the robots than some company renting them to us at whatever price it likes. If the farm owns them, the savings can go into shorter weeks and better pay. That's the deal I'd put to the trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Marek agree with this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's keener than me, honestly. He's been bored at his job for a year. The risk is we both bet on the same thing, so I'd want to keep the savings separate from the business.

say: I'd say there's time for community farms to **own their robots**.
I'd pitch a **shared machine pool** to other community farms.
think: Privately five years lets Marek **move into farm robotics** by choice.
At 32 and 35 I'm young enough to **change my role**.
do: Take a full **online robotics** engineering course this year.
Set up a **robot pool** with three farms, Greenhollow funding a third.
Have Marek **freelance** for farm-tech firms while salaried.
feel: She feels **uneasy** but more **interested** than afraid.
S3.quote: I'd rather the crew's farm owns the robots than some company renting them to us at whatever price it likes.
fieldNote: Five years turns her from crisis mode to **building** mode.
She ties automation savings to **shorter weeks** and better pay.
She spots the risk of the couple **betting on one thing**.
Her timing logic explicitly uses the **3-year robot lag**.

steps.text: Complete an online agricultural robotics engineering course
Fund a third of a shared robot pool with three farms
Have Marek freelance for farm-tech firms while still salaried

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Then it's a career change, not a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do it well, if we start the rules and the ownership now. I'd push the regional farmers' network to set up a training scheme that every farm worker can use. That'd be my main public line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the one I'd be most comfortable with. I'd be 37 for AGI and 40 for the robots, which sounds old, but I'd have spent a decade getting ready. My worry is that people around me would treat ten years as forever and do nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running Greenhollow as it is for now, and build the second polytunnel after all. I'd lobby the regional council for a robot co-op fund in the next budget round. And I'd put some of my grandmother's money into a farm-tech co-op as a member, not a speculator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Uneasy about the people who won't move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you thinking of when you say the people who won't move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yusuf, mainly, and a couple of the older growers in the network. Yusuf's 50 and brilliant with pigs, and he's told me he'll retire before he works with a robot. I'd want him to have a real choice, not just a pushed one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any family plans tied to that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about kids around 30. With ten years' warning I wouldn't change our plan for kids, and with two years I'd have waited. That's probably the clearest difference for me between the pictures.

say: I'd say a decade is enough **if we start** the rules now.
I'd push for a **training scheme** for every farm worker in the region.
think: Privately this is the scenario I'm **most comfortable** with.
I worry others will treat ten years as **forever**.
do: Build the **second polytunnel** and run Greenhollow as normal.
Lobby the council for a **robot co-op fund** next budget.
Invest some of the **inheritance** in a farm-tech co-op as a member.
feel: She feels mostly **calm**, and **uneasy** about people who won't move.
S4.quote: With ten years' warning I wouldn't change our plan for kids, and with two years I'd have waited.
fieldNote: The warning time directly changes her **family timing**.
Her concern shifts to **Yusuf** and older growers who won't adapt.
She invests as a **co-op member**, keeping her values in her money.
Long horizon reads to her as a **career change**, not a crisis.

steps.text: Build the second polytunnel and keep the current crew
Lobby the regional council for a robot co-op fund
Join a farm-tech co-op as a member with inheritance money

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits Marek first and then me three years later, with no time to build anything. What would help is a robot dividend, so the gains get shared, and public loans for community farms to own their machines instead of renting them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who eats. Robots could make food cheaper, or they could make a few companies rich. A robot that picks carrots is only good news if the family buying the carrots can still afford them.

headlineQuote: A robot that picks carrots is only good news if the family buying the carrots can still afford them.
portrait: Daria is 27 and manages a **community-supported** farm owned by a land trust, living with Marek, a **software developer**.
She uses **AI tools daily** for crop planning and is keen to automate quickly.
Her biggest exposure is through **Marek's coding job**, which shrinks first in faster scenarios.
She answers change with **shared ownership** of robots and a business plan with Marek.
Mood runs from **calm** in slow worlds to **alarmed** when both incomes face the 2028 timeline.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which takes Marek's **job** first and hers three years later.
whatWouldHelp: A **robot dividend** and public **loans** for community farms to own machines.
